# The slow road to the press

Every autumn we load the first barge at Hollin Vale with forty tonnes of cider apples and send it down the canal to the press at Stannard Lock. The trip takes nine hours, which is about six hours longer than a lorry would need. People ask me why we still do it this way, and I think the honest answer starts with the fruit, with the boat a long way second.

A cider apple bruises if you look at it wrong. On a lorry the crates shake on every pothole between the orchard gate and the main road, and the bottom layer arrives soft. On the water the crates barely move at all. When we weighed the waste last year, the barge loads lost a little over two percent to bruising and the lorry loads lost closer to nine. That gap pays for the slow trip several times over -- and it pays the growers, not us.

The second reason is the towpath. Our barges are pulled by a small electric tug that we charge from the panels on the old lock keeper's cottage. A lot of people picture something romantic when they hear about it, a horse and a painted boat. The reality is a grey tug, a crew of two, and a spreadsheet of charging times that Mara keeps on the cottage wall. It is cheap, and it is quiet enough that the herons stay on the bank as we pass.

We started the co-op eleven years ago with three orchards and one borrowed boat. There are now nineteen orchards and four barges, and every grower owns an equal share regardless of how many trees they have. That rule has cost us at least one large member who wanted a bigger vote. I think we were right to let him go, though I still buy his perry at the market every spring.

The hard part has never been the canal. The hard part is the calendar. Apples ripen when they ripen. The press has its own schedule. The canal trust closes two locks for repairs every October whether we like it or not. Most years we lose a week to those repairs and spend it moving fruit by road after all. I would rather plan around that week honestly than pretend the water can do everything.

There is a version of this business that grows fast. We could lease more barges and run boats through the night. The big supermarket contract keeps arriving in my inbox. I have looked at the numbers more than once. Each time the plan needs us to buy fruit from outside the valley to fill the boats, and each time the growers vote it down. They want a co-op that carries their apples, and they are clear that it should stay that size.

So the growth we do take is slow. A new orchard joins when a current member vouches for it and the group agrees at the spring meeting. We buy a new barge only after three full seasons. I think that rhythm frustrates some of our younger members, who see the demand and want to meet it this year. I understand that, and I also remember the winter we nearly folded because we had bought a boat we could not fill.

What I want people to take from all this is simple. The canal is a tool, the same as the tug and the spreadsheet. It suits fruit that bruises, a group that votes, and a valley that would like fewer lorries on its lanes. When any of those stops being true, we should be the first to say so.

Until then, the first barge leaves on the second Monday of October. If you are on the towpath that morning, wave at the crew -- they have been up since four.
